title: Why We Built a GlusterFS Repository for EL10, Rolling Releases, and Containers
summary: GlusterFS is already packaged by several Linux distributions. Eliware is focused on the gaps we found around EL10-compatible RPMs, rolling builds, container images, and inspectable release metadata.
author: Eliware
content:
# Why We Built a GlusterFS Repository for EL10, Rolling Releases, and Containers

GlusterFS is not impossible to obtain. Fedora packages it through its normal package ecosystem, and Debian and Ubuntu provide GlusterFS packages for their supported releases. If you run one of those distributions, the first step may simply be enabling the appropriate repository component and installing the packages your system provides.

Our problem was more specific. For EL10-compatible systems, finding a current and straightforward GlusterFS package path was much harder. We also did not find a single, cohesive distribution path that combined EL10-compatible RPMs, clearly labeled rolling builds, runtime container images for multiple operating-system targets, validation evidence, and immutable artifact references.

That is the gap Eliware is trying to fill.

## We are not replacing upstream GlusterFS

GlusterFS is an upstream open-source project with its own community, source repository, documentation, and release process. Eliware is building a packaging and distribution layer around selected GlusterFS builds.

That distinction matters. We do not want users to confuse an Eliware package, image, or repository with the upstream project itself. The upstream project remains the source of the filesystem. Our job is to make selected artifacts easier to obtain, evaluate, and identify on the platforms we target.

For upstream information, use the official [GlusterFS source repository](https://github.com/gluster/glusterfs), [release history](https://github.com/gluster/glusterfs/releases), and [Gluster documentation](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/).

## The EL10 packaging problem

EL10-compatible environments are important to the infrastructure teams we work with. They are also a place where package availability has not always matched what operators need from a current storage project.

When a package path is missing or unclear, an operator is left with unattractive choices:

- build GlusterFS from source and own the full packaging problem;
- use an older package that does not match the desired release;
- assemble packages from unrelated sources; or
- move the workload to a different operating system solely to obtain a convenient artifact.

Those choices may all be valid in the right circumstances. They are not a satisfying default for someone who wants a repeatable EL10-compatible installation.

Eliware began with EL10-compatible RPMs because that was the gap we encountered most directly. The repository is intended to provide a clearer path for installing and evaluating GlusterFS on current EL10-oriented infrastructure.

## What already exists elsewhere

It is important to describe the ecosystem fairly. Fedora currently publishes GlusterFS packages, including GlusterFS 11.2 builds. Debian publishes GlusterFS packages across supported suites and backports, and Ubuntu provides GlusterFS packages for supported releases through its package ecosystem.

Those distribution packages are useful and may be exactly the right choice for users of those operating systems. Eliware is not claiming that every user needs a separate repository.

Our observation is narrower:

> Package availability is not uniform across operating systems, and the availability of a package does not automatically provide a coordinated container, rolling-release, validation, and provenance story.

That is where we see room to contribute. [Fedora’s package index](https://packages.fedoraproject.org/pkgs/glusterfs/glusterfs/), [Debian’s package search](https://packages.debian.org/search?keywords=glusterfs), and [Ubuntu’s package search](https://packages.ubuntu.com/search?keywords=gluster) show the existing distribution paths.

## Stable packages for predictable installations

The first requirement is unglamorous: packages should be installable and identifiable. Stable artifacts follow released GlusterFS versions and are intended for users who want a predictable package source for an installation or evaluation environment.

A stable lane should make it easy to answer:

- Which GlusterFS version is this?
- Which operating system and architecture does it target?
- Which packages are included?
- Where did the source come from?
- What validation did the candidate pass?

The repository publishes metadata and release records alongside the package indexes so the filename is not the only information an operator has.

## Rolling builds for people who need to test ahead

Stable packages are not the only useful packages. Storage operators, distribution maintainers, application developers, and upstream contributors sometimes need to evaluate changes before they appear in a stable release.

That is the purpose of a rolling lane. It follows upstream development or a selected current revision and makes the result available for testing. It is clearly labeled so it is not mistaken for a stable package.

Rolling does not mean untested. It means the input is moving. The validation process still checks installation and core lifecycle behavior, but users should understand that an upstream development build may change and may not be appropriate for a long-lived production installation.

The distinction is simple:

```text
stable  = choose predictability
rolling = choose earlier evaluation
```

Both choices should be explicit.

## Packages are only one deployment format

Many infrastructure teams now evaluate software in more than one way. A package may be right for a traditional server, while a container is useful for a test cluster, a Kubernetes deployment, or a reproducible development environment.

That is why the project publishes runtime images as part of the distribution plan. A container image can provide:

- a known operating-system base;
- a known GlusterFS package set;
- consistent runtime dependencies;
- a repeatable service layout; and
- an immutable digest that identifies the exact image content.

The image does not remove the need to understand storage. A containerized GlusterFS node still needs persistent brick storage, stable identity, correct network reachability, host security configuration, and a tested recovery procedure. It simply provides another controlled way to assemble and evaluate the runtime.

## Multiple operating-system targets

A practical packaging project should meet users where they run infrastructure. Our initial focus is EL10-compatible RPMs, but the broader repository model includes Debian-family repositories and runtime images targeted at different operating-system environments.

The purpose is not to make every artifact identical. Distribution packaging has real differences in filesystem layout, service integration, dependencies, security policy, and lifecycle conventions. The purpose is to make those differences visible while providing a consistent place to find the relevant artifact and its metadata.

A user should not have to infer from a container tag or package filename whether an artifact is intended for a particular operating-system family. Target, architecture, version, release lane, and image identity should be clear.

## What makes this different from a package mirror?

A package mirror copies artifacts. A distribution pipeline should explain and test how those artifacts came to exist.

The Eliware pipeline is built around several connected pieces:

- source revision tracking;
- distribution-specific package builds;
- package smoke tests;
- clean-environment installation and lifecycle tests;
- runtime-image validation;
- signed repository metadata and packages;
- provenance records; and
- immutable image digests.

This does not make the artifacts universally correct. It makes the release process more inspectable and gives operators evidence to evaluate.

For a detailed look at the process, read [How We Build, Test, Sign, and Publish GlusterFS Packages](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/).

## Why provenance belongs beside the package

A package version tells you what software it claims to contain. It does not necessarily tell you which source revision, base image, build environment, validation run, or publication generation produced it.

Our release records connect those pieces. For a published generation, we want users to be able to ask:

- Which upstream revision produced this artifact?
- Which operating-system input was used?
- Did the package install in a clean environment?
- Did a test volume complete its lifecycle?
- Which image digest corresponds to the runtime image?
- Were repository metadata and packages signed?

Those questions become particularly important for storage software. An operator may need to reproduce an installation months later, compare a stable package with a rolling build, or identify exactly what was running during an incident.

## What we are not claiming

We are not claiming that Fedora, Debian, or Ubuntu package GlusterFS poorly. Their package ecosystems are valuable, maintained distribution paths, and many users should continue using them.

We are not claiming that a rolling build is production-ready merely because it passed a smoke test.

We are not claiming that a container image eliminates the operational work of running a distributed filesystem. Brick placement, networking, backups, security policy, healing, monitoring, and failure testing still matter.

We are not claiming to speak for upstream GlusterFS.

And we are not claiming that Eliware’s experimental deployment architecture is suitable for every environment.

The claim is more practical: there is value in making current EL10-compatible artifacts, rolling evaluations, multi-target images, and release evidence easier to find together.

## A repository for the gaps between ecosystems

The Linux distribution ecosystem is strongest when each project can focus on what it does well. Fedora, Debian, Ubuntu, and other distributions integrate software into their own release and maintenance systems. Upstream GlusterFS develops the filesystem. Users choose the path that best matches their operating system and operational requirements.

Eliware can contribute in the spaces that are not consistently covered by those paths:

```text
EL10-compatible RPMs
          +
clearly labeled rolling builds
          +
container images for multiple targets
          +
validation and provenance
          =
A more complete evaluation path for GlusterFS
```

That is the repository we wanted when we started building our own storage infrastructure. It is the repository we are now making available to others.

## Start with the path that fits

If you run Fedora, Debian, or Ubuntu, first check the packages available from your distribution. They may be the simplest and best-supported option for your environment.

If you need an EL10-compatible RPM path, want to evaluate a rolling GlusterFS build, or prefer a validated runtime image, visit the [Eliware GlusterFS Repository](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/).

Start with the [EL10 installation and first-volume guide](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/), read about [replica 3 and its limits](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/), and test the exact storage and network behavior your environment requires.

Our goal is not to make GlusterFS sound effortless. It is to make the software easier to obtain, easier to evaluate, and easier to identify exactly when you run it.
